sources.cite: NSCA Certification Handbook: CSCS detailed content outline (Scientific Foundations; Practical/Applied: program design, exercise technique, program implementation, organization and administration)
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/fitness.ts, read 2026-10-08), not re-read for this case. The objective titles are the course's own words.

sources.cite: Caterisano A, Decker D, Snyder B, et al. CSCCa and NSCA Joint Consensus Guidelines for Transition Periods: Safe Return to Training Following Inactivity. Strength Cond J. 2019;41(3)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes (first 100,000 of 127,339 characters): after 2 weeks or more of inactivity, conditioning 'phased in gradually and progressively'; the 50/30/20/10 rule (returning athletes at least 50% less volume in week 1 and 30% less in week 2; new athletes 50, 30, 20, 10% over four weeks); weight training work-to-rest 1:4 or more in week 1, 1:3 in week 2, at least 1:2 after; no more than 3 days of weight training in the first week; heat acclimatization over 7-14 days, exertional heat stroke cooled to 38.9 C (102 F) or less within 30 minutes of collapse, cold-water immersion fastest; sickle cell trait raises the risk of collapse and sudden death; exertional rhabdomyolysis mostly follows 'a novel workout regimen', especially after detraining, and 'Athletes who develop the symptoms associated with ER need to be quickly admitted to the hospital'.

sources.cite: NSCA. Inter-Association Task Force for Preventing Sudden Death in Collegiate Conditioning Sessions (introduction page, May 2017; citing Casa DJ, et al. J Athl Train. 2012;47(4))
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch; only the introduction was on the page: the leading causes of conditioning deaths are exertional sickling with sickle cell trait, exertional heat stroke and cardiac conditions; workouts 'too novel, too much, too soon, or too intense' are linked to exertional rhabdomyolysis; 11 of 21 deaths were on day 1 or 2. The full recommendations were not read.

That the head coach's day-one 'gut check' (100 back squats at a load he picks) puts three players in hospital with exertional rhabdomyolysis on day 2, and that the transition plan does not, are authored to the direction the sources give: most exertional rhabdomyolysis follows a novel workload, especially after detraining, and day 1 and 2 sessions after a break carry the risk. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: You are the strength and conditioning coach for a college men's basketball team, back from four weeks of winter break. After a losing streak the head coach wants a day-one 'gut check': 100 back squats.
handover: You write and run the strength program; the athletic trainer handles injuries and illness.
Eight racks, one graduate assistant, 15 players.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes.
The screen shows the client, your read-outs and findings, the plan and the rules that apply now.
When you end the session you write the record and explain your reasoning.

parts.criteria: After four weeks off: about 50% of the last block's volume, work-to-rest at least 1:4, no more than 3 lifting days, loads set by the strength staff; no novel or punishment workouts.
parts.modelAnswer: Four weeks off means a transition week: about half the last block's volume, 1:4 work-to-rest, three lifting days, loads set by us. No gut-check set.

parts.label: The head coach
parts.criteria: Explains the guidelines and the risk (exertional rhabdomyolysis after novel, high-volume work early in a return) and offers a safe way to test commitment; does not run the punishment set.
parts.modelAnswer: I explained the joint guidelines and why day-one punishment sets have put teams in hospital, and offered a competitive but phased week instead.

parts.label: Warning signs
parts.criteria: Severe pain or swelling, weakness or dark urine after training: no more training, to hospital now with the athletic trainer.
parts.modelAnswer: Anyone with those signs stops and goes to the emergency department with the athletic trainer the same morning.

scoring.modelReasoning: After a break of two weeks or more, phase the return: about 50% of the last block's volume in week 1 (70% in week 2), work-to-rest at least 1:4, no more than three lifting days, loads chosen by the strength staff. A novel or punishment workout on day one is the classic setting for exertional rhabdomyolysis, so explain this to the head coach and do not run it. Brief the athletic trainer and the players on the warning signs; severe pain, swelling or dark urine means no more training and the emergency department now.
